sections.heading: Weld integrity
sections.text:
Air flow passing over the weld may interfere with shielding mechanisms and potentially compromise weld integrity. Consequently, there is a tendency for boilermakers to prefer areas of low air movement when setting up to weld, and there is a reluctancy to introduce additional air movement close to the point of welding. Testing conducted on welding fume extraction hoods and on-tool exhaust systems have demonstrated that weld integrity should not be adversely impacted by introducing controlled ventilation at flow rates up to 0.5 m/s for most conventional gas-shielded arc welding methods.
When welding is conducted with the weld tip and gas shield shroud positioned inside small cavities with limited volumes of air, the flow rate on LEV systems may need to be adjusted to prevent the removal of shielding gas.
For example, some on-tool systems have a local bypass valve to enable the boilermaker to manually restrict the extraction ventilation flow during welding in small spaces. Some also have flow meters to test and calibrate the exhaust flow rate and the shield gas supply flow rate, to ensure optimal performance.

sections.heading: Maintenance of ventilation controls
sections.text:
The performance and effectiveness of ventilation systems depends on how well they are maintained, and this requires regular periodic inspections and servicing.
A daily prestart operational check should be conducted prior to use of the ventilation control. For LEV this should include the following:
• Visual inspection of inlet, hood, hosing/ducting for visible damage
• Visual inspection of condition of filter media and change where required.
• Turn on LEV and check air is drawing across inlet/hood.
Exhaust ventilation systems should be designed and equipped with the required pressure gauges, flow meters, and/or alarm indicators, to enable ongoing performance checks in-service and periodic maintenance inspections. This is required for ongoing control effectiveness verification.
Ventilation control equipment should be incorporated into the mine’s scheduled preventive maintenance program, and work order system, requiring inspections at least every 12 months (AIOH n.d.). The results of inspection and measurement should be recorded and rescheduled within specified intervals. The key maintenance inspection requirements for on-tool exhaust systems and fume exhaust hoods have been listed below.
An example of a scheduled maintenance inspection checklist for exhaust ventilation systems has been provided in Appendix G.

sections.heading: On-tool exhaust systems
sections.text:
• Visual inspection of inlet nozzle for obstructions, vacuum hose for holes and/or deformation.
• Visual inspection of filter media and housing for signs of breakthrough, by-pass and/or build-up of surface deposition and verification of filter replacement frequency.
• The volume flow rate at the extraction nozzle(s) should be measured and compared with exhaust specification.
• Back pressure drop across the filter media should be measured and compared with specification.
• Shield gas supply flow rate should be measured and checked against specification.

sections.heading: Fume exhaust hoods
sections.text:
• Visual inspection of hood and face inlet for obstructions and damage.
• Visual inspection of flexible and rigid ducting for damage, collapse and/or penetration holes.
• Visual inspection of filter media and housing for signs of breakthrough, by-pass and/or build-up of surface deposition and verification of filter replacement frequency.
• Face velocity across the hood face inlet surface area should be measured and compared with specification, for example using a hot-wire anemometer
• Back pressure drop across the filter media should be measured and compared with specification.
Where faults are found on inspection the ventilation control equipment should be removed from service and repaired. Interim controls should be implemented until the device is back in service.

sections.heading: Administrative Controls
sections.text:
Task Rotation For prolonged high-exposure tasks, rotation should be considered to minimise individual exposure duration.
However, rotation may be limited by the availability of workers with appropriate qualifications and skills to perform competent welding. In many cases, the most experienced or efficient worker performs the majority of the tasks. Where feasible, rotation should be planned and documented.

sections.heading: Worker Positioning
sections.text: Positioning of the welder’s head away from the fume can reduce potential exposure. For example, set up and position the welder’s head and breathing zone upwind of the fume’s direction of flow or move work pieces to the side where possible. Further information on positioning is provided in Fume Minimisation Guidelines (Appendix J)

sections.heading: Welding Methods and Procedures
sections.text:
The site’s SHMS should include safe operating procedures (SOPs) for managing hazards associated with hot work activities including welding. As a minimum, these should incorporate the following.
For hot work and welding procedures:
• identify welding fume and gases as key hazards
• specify what types of ventilation controls will be applied to each task (e.g., on-torch extraction, fume hoods, ducted exhaust systems)
• what administrative controls will be applied (e.g., welder positioning and job scheduling)
• list of the minimum respiratory protection requirements (including filtration class) for hot work and welding activities
• specify what fume controls will be applied for welding in confined spaces (e.g. ventilation plans Appendix H)
• outline the training requirements for hot work, including induction and refresher frequency
• consider fume dispersion mapping, to assess the potential exposure to trade assistants or other workers positioned adjacent to the welder. This supports more informed decisions around task positioning and timing.
Hot work permits should specify:
• the type(s) of hot work activity being undertaken
• the types of ventilation controls to be put in place
• the type and level of respiratory protection to be used.

sections.heading: Training and Competency
sections.text: Training packages on welding fume hazards, control measures, and correct PPE use, should be developed and delivered to all boilermakers performing hot work activities at the mine. Refer to Section 9 below for further details.

sections.heading: Respiratory Protection Equipment (RPE)
sections.text:
RPE is the least effective form of hazard control on the hierarchy of controls. The objective should be to, wherever possible, reduce exposures to below the OEL and to as low as reasonably achievable, without considering the potential protection afforded by RPE. Every effort should be made to control exposures by higher order controls before considering the use of RPE.
However, currently, where welding and other hot work processes are conducted on mine sites, the concentration of fume and gas generated will require the wearing of RPE in addition to engineering and other higher order controls, to protect the boilermaker from exposures above recommended exposure limits.
The mine is required to have a SOP outlining how to use PPE for tasks at the mine and this is to include training on selecting and using RPE. The PPE SOP should specify the type of respiratory protection required to be worn for different types of hot work activities including welding at the mine, and other minimum requirements including facial fit testing and training.
There are a range of suitable respiratory protection types available for protecting the boilermaker from exposure to welding fume. These range from negative pressure disposable and reusable half face masks to PAPR and air-supplied head coverings/helmets connected to a compressed air supply.
There are a broad range of different product manufacturers for each type of respirator and examples of commonly used RPE types are detailed in the RSHQ fact sheet on RPE and Respiratory protective equipment at work (Health and Safety Executive 2013).
Disposable half face masks suitable for welding fume include P2 or P3 particulate filters and are impregnated with carbon/charcoal to remove nuisance gases. These are negative pressure RPE, and quantitative facial fit testing is required for the individual wearer to ensure correct size and shape is selected for the individual.
Figure 26: Example of commonly used disposable half face RPE Reusable half face masks provide a higher level of facial fit/seal and enable higher capacity filter cartridges to be used. These facepieces should be fitted with filter cartridges rated for welding protection. As a minimum this should include P2 or P3 Class filters. Organic A Class filters, Aus Class or nuisance/ odour organic filters may be used for certain applications. Gas filters should always be fitted in addition to and in combination with particulate (P2 or P3) filters and never in isolation. Particulate filters are always required to remove welding fume. These are negative pressure RPE and quantitative facial fit testing should be conducted on individual wearers to ensure corrected size and shape RPE is selected for the individual.
Figure 27: Example of commonly used reusable half face RPE Powered air purifying respirators (PAPR) are typically incorporated into a welding style helmet/face shield, where the fan and filter assembly are mounted onto a belt and the filtered air is supplied through a hose connected into the back of the helmet. The filtered air is supplied into the helmet at a specified minimum flow rate (usually 170 lpm) in order to maintain positive pressure inside the loose fitting head covering/helmet. The filter housing is capable of fitting particulate P2 or P3 filter cartridges alone or in combination
Figure 28: Example of with nuisance/ odour or A Class organic gas filter cartridges. commonly used PAPR When well maintained, PAPRs are highly effective in providing protection for the boilermaker. Their use is not recommended in confined spaces where air-supplied systems are preferred.
Limitations: The performance of PAPR welding helmets depends on the integrity of each of the many components and this requires regular maintenance inspections. In practice, the protection provided by PAPR is typically compromised when:
• there are leaks or obstructions in the hose connecting and delivering filtered air to the helmet
• the flow rate delivered into the helmet falls below the minimum required to maintain positive pressure
• facial seals are loose and allow inward leakage into the breathing zone.
Air supplied or air-line respirators typically use the same loose fitting welding style helmet/face shield used for PAPR, except the belt mounted fan and filtration assembly is replaced with a low pressure air-line for connection back to a regulated compressor outlet. An in-line filter assembly including particulate, water vapour and oil trap, is installed between the compressor and respirator to prevent contaminants from the compressor entering the respirator. The air-line configuration should be regularly tested for conformance with the minimum air quality requirements specified in AS 1715:2009 (Standards Australia 2009). Testing is typically performed at 6 or 12 month intervals depending on the intensity of use.

sections.heading: Maintenance/Inspection Checklist Daily pre-start inspection:
sections.text:
Disposable masks (e.g. P2):
• conduct a fit check every time the mask is worn
• discard after each use
• replace multiple times per shift if required (e.g. visibly soiled, wet, or damaged).
Reusable masks (Half/Full Face/PAPR):
• inspect before each use for damage
• check inhalation/exhalation valves (where appropriate)
• conduct a fit check every time the mask is worn
• clean after each use (daily or weekly depending on use frequency)
• ensure battery fully charged (where appropriate)
• store in a clean, dry, sealed container when not in use
• date-stamp and track filter cartridge replacements.
Filter Replacement Guidelines:
• Particulate Filters (P2/P3): Replace when visibly soiled and/or breathing resistance increases (typically weekly or monthly depending on weld intensity).
• Gas Cartridges: Replace within 6 months after opening sealed packaging (even if not used), and after approximately 1-4 weeks of use, depending on weld intensity, or sooner if breakthrough smell or odour is detected.
• Filter cartridges should not be used after the expiry date stated by the manufacturer/supplier, on the filter packaging.

sections.heading: 3–6 Monthly Planned Maintenance PAPR Assemblies:
sections.text:
• add to site’s planned equipment maintenance register for inspection every 3–6 months as a work order
• inspect entire unit (hood, hose, filters, battery) for function and wear
• test airflow and battery performance
• document maintenance actions.
An example of a planned 3-6 monthly maintenance inspection checklist has been attached in Appendix F:
PAPR checklist.
All CMWs required to wear respiratory protection should be trained in the selection, use, maintenance and limitations of these devices. As a minimum this should include:
• donning and doffing the facepiece
• visually inspecting for faults and damage
• conducting a fit check
• how and when to replace filters (including both particulate and gas filter types)
• clean shaven requirements for close fitting facepieces
• completing an individual facial fit test to select the correct size and type of respirator.

sections.heading: Confined space
sections.text:
Welding in confined spaces within coal mining environments presents significant risks due to the potential accumulation of toxic gases and fumes, heat stress, and reduced oxygen levels, and should therefore be considered in the hazard identification phase. Each task must be assessed and managed on a case-by-case basis, as conditions can vary widely depending on the location, materials, and ventilation available.
It is essential where hot work/welding activities are to be performed, that welding fume is clearly identified as a hazard and acknowledged on the confined space entry permit, and that a site-specific ventilation plan is developed and implemented to ensure the safe dilution and extraction of fumes and gases.
An example of ventilation plan drawings applied to shutdown welding work conducted inside a dragline, is provided in Appendix H.
The specific types of welding methods and ventilation controls being applied to control welding fume inside the confined space should be clearly identified and documented in the risk assessment, hot work permit, and confined space entry permit. The types of respiratory protection and filtration media required to be worn inside the confined space to protect CMWs from welding fume exposure should also be clearly documented in these permits.

sections.heading: Conducting health surveillance for welding fume
sections.text:
The SSE and employers have obligations for ensuring the health surveillance of coal mine workers identified as being likely to be exposed to welding fume. The purpose of health surveillance is to:
• monitor for changes to a worker’s health from baseline at the earliest opportunity
• implement early intervention measures to protect workers’ health
• ensure that exposure controls and monitoring programs are effective.
Health surveillance shall be carried out by, or under the supervision of, an appointed medical adviser (AMA) under the CMWs’ Health Scheme (the Scheme). The Scheme has been optimised to detect occupational lung disease early and ensures health examinations are performed to the required standards by appropriately qualified and experienced medical providers approved and regulated by RSHQ. It also ensures medical records are stored and maintained in an appropriate form, enabling comparative assessment to previous results.
Employers must undertake particular steps in the health assessment process in ResHealth to ensure welding fume health surveillance is completed for each worker likely to be exposed to welding fume. Employers must ensure that exposure to welding fume is one of the hazards they identify in the employer section of the assessment. For workers identified as at risk of exposure to welding fume, health surveillance should be completed:
• before a worker commences work that may involve exposure to welding fume
• at frequencies specified under the Scheme, or as advised by the AMA. and with consideration of the following:
• any personal exposure monitoring results
• specific welding fume tasks/exposures
• duration, frequency and level of exposure for workers
• effectiveness of engineering controls
• respiratory protection use (type and frequency of use).
As part of completing health surveillance, the AMAs may request and consider personal exposure monitoring results for welding fume, from the mine for relevant SEGs. The SSE and employer should facilitate the reporting of welding fume exposure monitoring results where requested by the AMA, to support the health surveillance process. _______ Online system for the health assessment process under the Coal Mine Workers’ Health Scheme

sections.heading: Education on Welding Fume
sections.text:
The mine’s SHMS should document the training needs analysis for all CMWs involved in welding activities, to include education on welding fume health impacts and controls relevant to their mine. This should include initial training at induction to the site and job, as well as ongoing periodic refresher training.
Those CMWs requiring education on welding fume and controls should include:
• persons authorised to carry out welding activities
• supervisors of welding activities
• other CMWs who assist with welding activities, or who may be potentially exposed to welding fume. i.e. trade assistants, confined space stand-by person.
This education should include:
• the health effects of exposure to welding fume and the fume’s various components
• how to minimise welding fume in the boilermakers breathing zone, including where to stand/operator positioning
• hot work SOP and hot work permit requirements
• what pre-use checks you should make to ensure your welding equipment is working correctly.
• which tasks have a high risk of exposure at the mine (confined space, bucket repairs)
• how to use controls, including o how to check and maintain the performance of welding fume controls o how to position movable LEV to make sure it is in the right place as you work o what to do if a control fails (PAPR, ventilation).
• how to select, use and look after RPE and PPE
• the safety risks associated with welding activities
• exposure monitoring for welding fume in the workplace, including: o exposure limits for each potential component o exceedance investigation process.
• health surveillance included in coal mine workers’ health scheme.
In addition to the education outlined above, specific training and up-skilling of boilermakers may be required and should be considered, prior to introducing new fume control methods. This is to ensure the new control is applied effectively and any additional hazards introduced as a result of the change, are acknowledged and managed. For example, when substituting FCAW with MIG methods and/or using on-tool exhaust, for the first time.
Structured on-line courses are also available from a number of registered training providers and cover a range of topics from general awareness about welding hazards and best practice, to specific qualifications for welders and welding supervisors. For example, Weld Australia provides courses aligned with AS 1796 and AS2214.1, that are listed and accessible on their website.
Welding hazard awareness courses should be incorporated into the training needs analysis for welding supervisors, and for engineers and managers who oversee projects involving welding activities.
The site senior executive must ensure that welding activities are supervised to the extent necessary to ensure the appropriate level of competency as outlined under CMSHR s 85B Supervising workers.

sections.heading: Review
sections.text: The site’s SHMS should provide for the regular review and continuous improvement of provisions relating to welding fume management to ensure continued suitability, adequacy and effectiveness. The management review process shall ensure that the necessary information is collected to allow the mine to carry out this evaluation. This should include performance and maintenance records for welding fume controls and sufficient welding fume exposure data for similar exposure groups undertaking hot work activities. This review shall be documented.

sections.heading: Audit
sections.text:
The site’s welding fume management system should be subjected to regular audits to maintain relevance and ensure continuous improvement. The aim of the audit is to ensure that sections of the SHMS that relate to the monitoring and control of welding fume are effectively implemented and maintained. The audit should cover any associated risk assessments, hazard management plans, operating procedures, maintenance procedures (e.g.
LEV and RPE), training records and personal exposure monitoring programs implemented at the mine.
The audit should also include the implementation of critical controls applied to welding fume, where these have been identified within the mine’s PHMP for ‘airborne dust and any other airborne contaminants’ Where the maintenance program is found to be ineffective in managing the operating performance of critical control systems actions are to be captured and documented to ensure the required changes have been implemented to rectify the inefficiency.
The frequency of the audit program should be based on the risk of the hazard concerned and the results of previous audits. The mine should establish and maintain procedures for the identification, maintenance, and storage of records.

sections.text:

Soldering Soldering is a joining process where the melting temperature of the filler metal is less than 450°C, Mild Steel Mild steel, also referred to as low-carbon steel, is an iron alloy containing a relatively low carbon content—typically between 0.05% and 0.25% by weight. It also commonly contains manganese (0.3–0.9%) and silicon (~0.2%) and may contain trace amounts of other elements.
Mild steel is characterised by moderate strength, high ductility, and excellent weldability, making it the most widely used form of steel across industrial applications. Its popularity is driven by its versatility, workability, and low cost.
Various national and international specifications may fall under the general classification of mild steel—for example, AS/NZS 3678 Grade 250.

sections.heading: Appendix B: Welding fume composition/common welding types
sections.text:
Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW) GMAW, commonly referred to as “MIG”, uses a continuous solid wire electrode, which melts due to the heat of an electric arc shielded by either an inert gas (e.g. argon or helium) or an active gas (e.g. Carbon Dioxide (CO2) or an argon/CO2/Oxygen (O2) mixed gas). Fumes are generated mainly from the vaporisation of the electrode materials, the shielding gases used to protect the weld pool, and to a limited extent, the parent metal. The specific fume composition depends on the metals involved, such as carbon and carbonmanganese steel (e.g. mild steel), low alloy steel, or stainless steel. When working with mild steel, the fume cloud mostly contains a mixture of iron oxide, and manganese, and occasionally nickel. The fume from welding steels with low alloy consumables may also contain nickel and chromium.
Figure 29: Gas Metal Arc Welding (GMAW) or Metal Inert Gas Welding (MIG) Various parameters can affect the types and quantities of gases generated.
For example, all arc welding processes will generate O3 and NOx due to the effects of UV radiation on the ambient air, especially at higher amperages. For shielding gas containing CO2, carbon monoxide (CO) can also be formed within the arc.
NOTE: In Australia, the term MIG is commonly used to describe this process. ISO uses the terms MIG to refer to the process that uses an inert shielding gas and Metal Active Gas (MAG) is used to refer to the active shielding gas variant.

sections.heading: Flux-Cored Arc Welding (FCAW)
sections.text:
FCAW uses a tubular wire with a flux core, which serves multiple purposes such as providing shielding gas, stabilizing the arc and adding alloying elements to the weld metal. During welding, the flux decomposes, producing fumes and a gas shielding, while the high temperatures vaporize metals from both the wire and to a much lesser extent, the workpiece. These metal particles react with shielding gases to form oxides, which are a significant component of the welding fume. FCAW can use shielding gas or rely on the flux alone for protection. The fumes typically contain complex oxides, including iron oxides, manganese, nickel, and chromium, depending on the wire's composition.
All forms of the flux cored arc process and the GMAW or MIG process uses similar welding equipment (power source and wire feeder).
Figure 30: Flux-cored Arc Welding FCAW wire have classification which vary according to their strength and composition of the flux core. These are detailed in the following sections.
Gases typically evolved during flux cored welding include the components of any shielding gas used, O3, CO2/CO and some NOx.

sections.heading: Gas Shielded
sections.text:
Gas shielded flux cored welding uses a cored or tubular wire which is shielded by an active or mixed gas such as CO2 or an argon-based gas with 10-25% CO2 which may also contain small amounts of O2. The tubular wire will typically contain some fluxing compounds mixed with rutile (type T1 or T2 wires), or basic oxides and fluorides (“basic” or T5 wires). Rutile type wires have excellent all-positional running characteristics and are commonly used in Queensland’s coal mines.
Gas-shielded flux cored wires filled mainly with metal powders are described as “metal cored” (type T15). They are high deposition wires with running characteristics similar to those of the solid wire MIG process and are mainly used in the down hand or flat position.
Gas shielded flux cored wires produce elevated levels of welding fume, compared with gas metal arc MIG processes.

sections.heading: Self-Shielded
sections.text: Some flux cored wires do not require shielding gas and are described as either self-shielded or “gasless”. In addition to fluxing agents (e.g. oxides, borates, silicates, fluorides etc), these wires contain high levels of materials that either react with O2 (e.g. aluminium powder) or decompose in the arc (e.g. carbonates, fluorides etc) to form a gas shield mainly consisting of CO2/CO. Being self-shielded, they offer good weld pool protection in windy conditions. These consumables produce high levels of welding fume, when compared with gas shielded.

sections.heading: Manual Metal Arc Welding (MMAW)
sections.text:
MMAW also known as stick welding, uses a consumable electrode coated with metallic powders, minerals, fluxing agents and binders. When the electrode “burns” during welding, this coating either melts or decomposes, releasing gases and particulates that form a significant part of the fumes.
These fumes help stabilize the arc and protect the weld area.
Coating types contain cellulose (types EXX10 or EXX11) or a range of oxides, fluorides and metal powders depending on their classification.
The high temperature of the arc melts both the electrode and the workpiece, vaporizing metals that react with O2 to form metal oxides, which are visible as fumes. The fumes typically contain a mix of metallic oxides, such as iron and
Figure 31: Manual Metal Arc Welding manganese, and potentially hazardous elements like chromium and nickel, depending on the electrode composition. The electrode's composition and coating significantly influence the type and quantity of fumes produced. Gases typically formed include CO2, CO, O3 and oxide of nitrogen. MMAW is referred to as shielded metal arc welding or SMAW in the United States of America.

sections.heading: Gas Tungsten Arc Welding (GTAW)
sections.text:
In GTAW, also known as TIG welding, the tungsten electrode is protected by an inert gas such as argon or helium and not consumed in the weld. There are a number of variations on the process relating to the use of filler metals including the autogenous (no filler wire) and hot-wire (electric current passing through the filler wire) process, however the most common form is to add filler metal to the molten weld pool by dipping a hand-held rod into the molten pool. Due to the risk of electric shock, the boilermaker uses a technique that avoids direct contact between the filler rod and the arc.
Fumes are primarily produced from the vaporisation of the weld pool (i.e. a mix of filler wire, the metals being welded and any coatings present on them).
The intense heat of the welding arc can vaporise metal surfaces, which
Figure 32: Gas Tungsten Arc Welding condense into fine airborne particles, forming fumes. While the tungsten electrode typically does not contribute to fume formation because it doesn't melt. The inert shielding gas, often argon or helium, protects the weld area from atmospheric gases but does not directly create fumes. High temperatures in GTAW can lead to the formation of metal oxides, especially when welding materials like aluminium, which can produce noticeable white smoke. The use of filler materials can also contribute to fumes, with the specific metals in the filler (such as chromium, nickel, or manganese) determining the fume composition and quantity. This process typically produces very low levels of fume.
Gases evolved by the process are mainly O3 and some NOx due to the effect of the UV radiation on O2 in the ambient air.

sections.heading: Air Arc Gouging
sections.text:
Air-arc gouging is a thermal gouging process that uses an arc from copper coated carbon electrode and a stream of compressed air to remove the molten metal and form a groove. The process runs at high amperage and produces high volumes of fumes. Fume composition is similar to the material being gouged with some traces of copper. Some gases are also created which consists of CO2/CO, O3 and NOx.
Figure 33: Air Arc Gouging

sections.heading: Plasma Cutting and Gouging
sections.text:
Plasma cutting and gouging is a thermal process that uses a constricted plasma arc where a high velocity jet of similar in composition to the material being cut or gouged with gases evolved being mainly O3 and some NOx.
Plasma cutting can occur on a cutting table or in some cases over a water table (or underwater) which captures most of the welding fume. Plasma cutting underwater is essentially fume-free.
Figure 34: Plasma cutting and gouging

sections.heading: Thermal Cutting and Gouging
sections.text:
Thermal cutting and gouging uses an O2/fuel gas (e.g. acetylene or Liquefied Petroleum Gas) mix to heat the metal being cut to ignition temperature. A jet of O2 causes the metal to oxidise and the molten swarf is removed by the cutting jet.
Particulates in the fume are oxides similar in composition to the material being cut or gouged. Gases emitted include the products of combustion and remnant O2 that is not consumed in the cutting or gouging process,

sections.heading: Brazing and Soldering
sections.text:
Brazing when used in Queensland coal mines can use either an O2/fuel gas flame or an electric arc process similar to GMAW or MIG (i.e. MIG Brazing). In all cases, unlike welding, the material being joined does not melt. Filler material that has a melting temperature >450°C is described as a brazing material and if <450°C, it is considered a soldering process.
Silver soldering is a process used within mines; however, it is a brazing process by definition. Fumes and gases emitted during brazing are minimal other than in arc brazing. Most braze alloys are copper based with silver solders for example having a range of copper/zinc/silver alloy compositions. Liquidus temperature for silver solders ranges from 655°C to 760°C depending on composition.

docs.title: Underground coal mines: VCD hatch seals

sections.heading: Front matter
sections.text: Underground coal mines:

sections.heading: Forward
sections.text:
On 22 May 2020 the Coroner delivered Inquest Findings into the death of Mr Paul McGuire . Mr McGuire died on 6 May 2014 when he attempted to enter a sealed goaf area of an underground coal mine. The air within the goaf was ‘irrespirable’ and had an oxygen concentration that would not support life.
The Coroner recommended that the Department establish a guideline of what may be considered in relation to preventing further ingress to the goaf during sealing up operations.
The Coroner also noted that the obligation is upon the individual mine operator to assess each individual circumstance to determine what is an appropriate design, and other relevant considerations for their hatch seals. They cannot abrogate their duty to the Department because it is their responsibility under the law to take the appropriate steps to protect all their coalmine workers.
The SSE shall ensure that the UMM includes the potential hazard of any persons entering an area of an underground mine that is being sealed in the risk assessment for this activity. This shall ensure the controls to prevent any potential further ingress of persons to the GOAF during and after the completion of sealing operations.
This guideline is intended to address the recommendation that the Coroner made in relation to the design and signage of hatches.

sections.heading: Purpose and Scope
sections.text:
This guideline provides information on life cycle requirements for ventilation control device (VCD) hatch seals. Guidance is provided on ways to minimise the risk of coal mine workers entering in an unauthorised manner a hatch and an irrespirable atmosphere.
It is up to the individual mine operator and Site Senior Executive (SSE) to assess each individual circumstance to determine what is an appropriate design, and other relevant considerations for their hatch seals. The guideline is not all-encompassing because there are so many different considerations at different mines, and the obligation rests with the mine operator to protect coal mine workers.

sections.heading: Hatch Seal
sections.text: A hatch is a ventilation control device inserted into a seal designed to assist conditioning of the goaf. A hatch includes a door inserted in a seal.

sections.heading: Goaf
sections.text: That part of a mine from which the coal has been partially or wholly extracted and then abandoned.

sections.heading: Risk Assessment
sections.text:
The mine must undertake a risk assessment of the seal and hatch seals:
• as per requirements of the Coal Mining Safety and Health Act 1999 and the Coal Mines Safety and Health Regulation 2017. Requirements of Division 5 Routine and Emergency Sealing of the Coal Mines Safety and Health Regulation 2017 must be addressed
• including all aspects of the seal and hatch seal life-cycle including design, construction, operation and maintenance
• risks associated with the potential for any persons entering or attempting to enter a hatch during or after the sealing up operations must be considered.

sections.heading: Safe Work procedure
sections.text:
Mines utilising hatch seals:
• shall develop and implement risk assessed safe work procedures which cover the life cycle of the hatch seal
• shall ensure that the construction of seals with hatches are constructed in accordance with the permit to construct a seal
• shall ensure that seal construction activities are supervised by an ERZ Controller
• should consider use of access permits for all work in around any hatch seal
• shall include procedures and processes that ensure seals and hatch seals are inspected by an ERZ Controller for dangerous gases prior to any work being undertaken in the vicinity of the seal
• persons or tradesmen who are not familiar with areas of the underground workings where the potential for accumulations of gases can request to be accompanied by a person appointed as an ERZ Controller. i.e. In an area of the mine where sealing of underground workings is being undertaken.

sections.heading: Design
sections.text:
Hatch seals are an integral part of the VCD seal design. Design and certification of a seal must include the hatch or hatches installed in the seal and as a minimum meet regulatory requirement as specified in Division 5; Routine and Emergency Sealing, Coal Mines Safety and Health Regulation 2017.
Each mine will have a unique combination of design requirements and durability hazards which need to be considered on a case by case basis.
Hatch seal designs must:
• meet regulatory requirements
• be designed and certified by suitably qualified and competent person
• be supported by risk assessments, engineering calculations, drawings and documentation assumptions, limitations, and conditions of use
• consider the need for the design to accommodate explosive conditions as well as a hydraulic head that may be imposed on the seal over the seal life
• consider other loads such as loads imposed by strata conditions that may impact on the integrity of the seal during its life cycle
• be resistant to fire as well as overpressure
• consider long term material selection, design loads, design life including environmental durability for example the impact of corrosive water, gases, accidental impact, spontaneous combustion
• the hatch seal should be sufficiently robust to resist flexing and distortion due to loads imposed during transport and installation
• include means to prevent unintended access through the hatch seal. This may be a fixed or lockable mesh insert in the hatch which prevents personnel access through the hatch void
• consider the hatch operational positions. Hatches may be open, closed or partially open.
Partially open hatches may be required during goaf purging operations. Means of securing the hatches in the selected positions to prevent inadvertent access shall be provided. This may be via the use of a secure lock such as a lock controlled by the ventilation officer or ERZ controller
• remain totally and permanently sealed when the hatch doors are closed
• have indelible warning signs or markings to indicate the danger of a potentially irrespirable atmosphere behind or adjacent to the hatch
• have signage that meets or exceeds requirements of the relevant Australian Standards.
The outer door of a typical hatch seal is shown in Figure 1. A hatch seal with a lockable mesh insert is shown in Figure 2.
Figure 1: Typical Hatch Seal
Figure 2: Hatch Seal fitted with a lockable mesh barrier

sections.heading: Installation
sections.text:
Factors to be considered include:
• the hatch seal shall be installed as per the designers’ instructions
• a seal construction certification process shall be in place at the mine to verify that the seal, including the hatch seal has been constructed and installed as per the design requirements
• when pipes are included in a seal for the purpose of future inertisation the pipes should be locked in the closed position to prevent inadvertent access or exposure to the goaf atmosphere
• once hatch is permanently closed it should be sealed in a manner that prevents any possibility of future opening (for example shotcrete over).

sections.heading: Barricades and signs
sections.text:
• Unauthorised access to the seal and hatch seal site should be restricted by a physical barricade and signs
• Sign posting alone should not be relied on to prevent unauthorised entry to behind the seal. Security devices such as locks and preferably fixed barriers should be installed. The fixed barrier may be of a temporary design such as a mesh wall. Use of only “No Road” tape is not an acceptable control
• Barricades should be signed indicating the potential consequence of an irrespirable atmosphere and the requirement of an ERZ controller to conduct an inspection prior to access
• A typical seal installation plan view showing a barricade and hatch seal to restrict entry to goaf areas is shown in Figure 3.
Door: remotely sealed area accessed For hatch detail refer Mesh barrier Insert A VCD Seal Hatch Door Barricade Insert A Ventilated roadway
Figure 3: Plan view of typical VCD seal and hatch

sections.heading: Operation
sections.text:
• A system of regular documented inspection of seals and hatch seals shall be implemented
• The inspection regime will be documented in the Standard Operating Procedure for Inspections
• The use of ventilation officer or ERZ controller’s locks to secure hatches in required operational positions to prevent inadvertent access shall be implemented
• Seals and hatch seal inspections by an ERZ Controller prior to workers entering a seal location should be used
• The inspection frequency shall be determined in accordance with the risk associated with the specified use of the hatch seals such as goaf purging operations where this may take an extended period of time before the goaf gases reach a stable point.
Specific detailed inspection and access controls must be implemented during goaf purging operations as a clear danger exists that persons may inadvertently access the hatch seals because they are not fully sealed.

sections.heading: Maintenance
sections.text: A documented maintenance program should be implemented which covers the life of the seal.

docs.title: Coal Mining Safety and Health Act 1999

sections.heading: Front matter
sections.text:
Queensland Coal Mining Safety and Health Act 1999 © State of Queensland 2026 This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License.
An Act to regulate the operation of coal mines, to protect the safety and health of persons at coal mines and persons who may be affected by coal mining operations, and for other purposes

sections.heading: Short title
sections.text: This Act may be cited as the Coal Mining Safety and Health Act 1999.

sections.heading: Commencement
sections.text: This Act commences on a day to be fixed by proclamation.

sections.heading: Act binds all persons
sections.text:
(1) This Act binds all persons, including the State and, so far as the legislative power of the Parliament permits, the Commonwealth and all the other States.
(2) Nothing in this Act makes the State liable to be prosecuted for an offence.

sections.heading: What does this Act apply to
sections.text: This Act applies to coal mines and coal mining operations.

sections.heading: Who does this Act apply to
sections.text:
This Act applies to—
(a) everyone who may affect the safety or health of persons while the persons are at a coal mine; and
(b) everyone who may affect the safety or health of persons as a result of coal mining operations; and
(c) a person whose safety or health may be affected while at a coal mine or as a result of coal mining operations.

sections.heading: Relationship with Rail Safety National Law (Queensland)
sections.text:
(1) This section applies if—
(a) this Act, in the absence of this section, would apply to a mining railway; and
(b) the Rail Safety National Law (Queensland) also applies to the mining railway.
(2) This Act does not apply to the mining railway to the extent that the Rail Safety National Law (Queensland) applies.
(3) In this section— mining railway means a railway that is in a mine other than a railway mentioned in the Rail Safety National Law (Queensland), section 7(1)(a).

sections.heading: Objects of Act
sections.text:
The objects of this Act are—
(a) to protect the safety and health of persons at coal mines and persons who may be affected by coal mining operations; and
(b) to require that the risk of injury or illness to any person resulting from coal mining operations be at an acceptable level; and
(c) to provide a way of monitoring the effectiveness and administration of provisions relating to safety and health under this Act and other mining legislation.

sections.heading: How objects are to be achieved
sections.text:
The objects of this Act are to be achieved by—
(a) imposing safety and health obligations on persons who operate coal mines or who may affect the safety or health of others at coal mines; and
(b) providing for safety and health management systems at coal mines to manage risk effectively; and
(c) making regulations and recognised standards for the coal mining industry to require and promote risk management and control; and
(d) establishing a safety and health advisory committee to allow the coal mining industry to participate in developing strategies for improving safety and health; and
(e) providing for safety and health representatives to represent the safety and health interests of coal mine workers; and
(f) providing for inspectors and other officers to monitor the effectiveness of risk management and control at coal mines, and to take appropriate action to ensure adequate risk management; and
(g) providing a way for the competencies of persons at coal mines to be assessed and recognised; and
(h) requiring management structures so that persons may competently supervise the safe operation of coal mines; and
(i) providing for an appropriate coal mines rescue capability; and
(j) providing for a satisfactory level of preparedness for emergencies at coal mines; and
(k) providing for the health assessment and health surveillance of persons who are, will be or have been coal mine workers.

sections.heading: Dictionary
sections.text: The dictionary in schedule 3 defines particular words used in this Act.

sections.heading: Meaning of coal mine
Meaning of on-site activities
Meaning of safety and health
sections.text: A person’s safety and health is the person’s safety or health, to the extent it is or may be affected by coal mining operations or other activities at a coal mine.

sections.heading: Meaning of competence
sections.text: Competence for a task at a coal mine is the demonstrated skill and knowledge required to carry out the task to a standard necessary for the safety and health of persons.

sections.heading: Meaning of consultation
sections.text: Consultation with coal mine workers is discussion between the site senior executive or supervisors and affected coal mine workers about a matter with the aim of reaching agreement about the matter.

sections.heading: Meaning of standard operating procedure
sections.text: A standard operating procedure at a coal mine is a documented way of working, or an arrangement of facilities, at the coal mine to achieve an acceptable level of risk, developed after consultation with coal mine workers.

sections.heading: Meaning of accident
sections.text: An accident at a coal mine is an event, or a series of events, at the coal mine causing injury to a person.

sections.heading: Meaning of serious accident
sections.text:
A serious accident at a coal mine is an accident at a coal mine that causes—
(a) the death of a person; or
(b) a person to be admitted to a hospital as an in-patient for treatment for the injury.

sections.heading: Meaning of high potential incident
sections.text: A high potential incident at a coal mine is an event, or a series of events, that causes or has the potential to cause a significant adverse effect on the safety or health of a person.

sections.heading: Meaning of risk
sections.text:
(1) Risk means the risk of injury or illness to a person arising out of a hazard.
(2) Risk is measured in terms of consequences and likelihood.

sections.heading: Meaning of hazard
sections.text: A hazard is a thing or a situation with potential to cause injury or illness to a person.

sections.heading: Meaning of principal hazard
sections.text: A principal hazard at a coal mine is a hazard at the coal mine with the potential to cause multiple fatalities.

sections.heading: Meaning of coal mine operator
sections.text:
(1) A coal mine operator for a coal mine is—
(a) the holder; or
(b) if another person has been appointed as the coal mine operator under section 53 and the appointment is notified to the chief inspector under section 49, the other person.
(2) If—
(a) another person mentioned in subsection (1)(b) is appointed as the coal mine operator for a separate part of a surface mine; and
(b) the appointment is notified to the chief inspector under section 49; the person’s responsibilities and safety and health obligations under this Act as a coal mine operator for a coal mine are limited to the separate part of the surface mine.
(3) If—
(a) 1 or more persons are appointed as coal mine operators for separate parts of a surface mine; and
(b) the appointments are notified to the chief inspector under section 49; the holder’s responsibilities and safety and health obligations under this Act as a coal mine operator for the coal mine are limited to the part of the mine to which the appointments do not apply.
(4) For this section, a part of a surface mine is taken to be a separate part of a surface mine only if—
(a) the part is geographically separated from the rest of the mine; and
(b) there is no physical overlapping of coal mining operations between the part and the operations in another part of the mine; and
(c) the coal mine operator for the part is in control of—
(i) the coal mining operations carried out in the part of the mine; and
(ii) the resources associated with the operations.
(5) A person may be appointed coal mine operator for more than 1 mine or separate part of a surface mine.

sections.heading: Meaning of geographically separated
Meaning of physical overlapping of coal mining
When is a coal mine operator not in control
sections.text:
For section 21(4), a coal mine operator is not in control of coal mining operations and associated resources for part of a surface mine if—
(a) a person involved with coal mining operations in the part of the mine can transfer resources to another part of the mine; or
(b) a person involved with coal mining operations in the part of the mine has the general management of another part of the mine; or
(c) a person involved in coal mining in the part of the mine can control the supply of services, including supervision and safety inspections, to another part of the mine.

sections.heading: Meaning of site senior executive
sections.text:
(1) The site senior executive for a coal mine is the most senior officer employed or otherwise engaged by the coal mine operator for the coal mine who—
(a) is located at or near the coal mine; and
(b) has responsibility for the coal mine.
(2) Subsection (1)(a) does not require an officer with responsibility for exploration activities under an exploration permit or mineral development licence to be located at or near the coal mine.
(3) If the officer only has responsibility for a separate part of a surface mine, the officer’s responsibilities and safety and health obligations under this Act as a site senior executive for a coal mine are limited to the separate part of the surface mine for which the officer has responsibility.

sections.heading: Meaning of supervisor
sections.text:
A supervisor at a coal mine is a person appointed under section 56 to—
(a) implement and monitor the coal mine’s safety and health management system; and
(b) give directions to other coal mine workers at the coal mine in accordance with the safety and health management system.

sections.heading: Meaning of industry safety and health representative
sections.text: An industry safety and health representative is a person who is appointed under section 109(1) to represent coal mine workers on safety and health matters and who performs the functions and exercises the powers of an industry safety and health representative mentioned in part 8, division 2.

crumbs.part: Part 2 The control and management of risk and other basic concepts

sections.heading: Meaning of site safety and health representative
sections.text: A site safety and health representative for a coal mine is a coal mine worker elected under section 93 by coal mine workers at the coal mine to exercise the powers and perform the functions of a site safety and health representative mentioned in part 7 division 2. of risk and other basic concepts

crumbs.part: Part 2 The control and management of risk and other basic concepts

sections.heading: What is an acceptable level of risk
sections.text:
(1) For risk to a person from coal mining operations to be at an acceptable level, the operations must be carried out so that the level of risk from the operations is—
(a) within acceptable limits; and
(b) as low as reasonably achievable.
(2) To decide whether risk is within acceptable limits and as low as reasonably achievable regard must be had to—
(a) the likelihood of injury or illness to a person arising out of the risk; and
(b) the severity of the injury or illness.

crumbs.division: Division 1 Control and management of risk

sections.heading: How is an acceptable level of risk achieved
sections.text:
(1) To achieve an acceptable level of risk, this Act requires that management and operating systems must be put in place for each coal mine.
(2) This Act provides that the systems must incorporate risk management elements and practices appropriate for each coal mine to—
(a) identify, analyse, and assess risk; and
(b) avoid or remove unacceptable risk; and
(c) monitor levels of risk and the adverse consequences of retained residual risk; and
(d) provide for critical controls; and
(e) investigate and analyse the causes of serious accidents and high potential incidents with a view to preventing their recurrence; and
(f) review the effectiveness of risk control measures, and take appropriate corrective and preventive action; and
(g) mitigate the potential adverse effects arising from residual risk.
(3) Also, the way an acceptable level of risk of injury or illness may be achieved may be prescribed under a regulation.

crumbs.part: Part 2 The control and management of risk and other basic concepts

sections.heading: What happens if the level of risk is unacceptable
sections.text:
(1) If there is an unacceptable level of risk to persons at a coal mine, this Act requires that—
(a) persons be evacuated to a safe location; and
(b) action be taken to reduce the risk to an acceptable level.
(2) Action to reduce the risk to an acceptable level may include stopping the use of specified plant or substances.
(3) The action may be taken by the coal mine operator for the mine, the site senior executive for the mine, industry safety and health representatives, site safety and health representatives, coal mine workers, inspectors or inspection officers.

crumbs.part: Part 2 The control and management of risk and other basic concepts

sections.heading: Cooperation to achieve objects of Act
sections.text:
(1) This Act seeks to achieve cooperation between coal operators, site senior executives and coal workers to achieve the objects of the Act.
(2) Cooperation is an important strategy in achieving the objects of the Act and is achieved—
(a) at an industry level by—
(i) the establishment of the coal mining safety and health advisory committee under part 6; and
(ii) the appointment of industry safety and health representatives under part 8; and
(b) at coal mine level by—
(i) the election of site safety and health representatives under part 7; and
(ii) the process of involving coal mine workers in the management of risk.

sections.heading: Obligations for safety and health
Discharge of obligations
sections.text:
A person on whom a safety and health obligation is imposed must discharge the obligation.
Maximum penalty—
(a) if the contravention caused multiple deaths—
(i) for an offence committed by a corporation—30,000 penalty units; or
(ii) for an offence committed by an officer of a corporation—6,000 penalty units or 3 years imprisonment; or
(iii) otherwise—3,000 penalty units or 3 years imprisonment; or
(b) if the contravention caused death or grievous bodily harm—
(i) for an offence committed by a corporation—15,000 penalty units; or
(ii) for an offence committed by an officer of a corporation—3,000 penalty units or 2 years imprisonment; or
(iii) otherwise—1,500 penalty units or 2 years imprisonment; or
(c) if the contravention caused bodily harm—
(i) for an offence committed by a corporation—7,500 penalty units; or
(ii) for an offence committed by an officer of a corporation—1,500 penalty units or 1 year’s imprisonment; or
(iii) otherwise—750 penalty units or 1 year’s imprisonment; or
(d) if the contravention involved exposure to a substance that is likely to cause death or grievous bodily harm—
(i) for an offence committed by a corporation—7,500 penalty units; or
(ii) for an offence committed by an officer of a corporation—1,500 penalty units or 1 year’s imprisonment; or
(iii) otherwise—750 penalty units or 1 year’s imprisonment; or
(e) otherwise—
(i) for an offence committed by a corporation—5,000 penalty units; or
(ii) for an offence committed by an officer of a corporation—1,000 penalty units or 6 months imprisonment; or
(iii) otherwise—500 penalty units or 6 months imprisonment. 35 Person may owe obligations in more than 1 capacity A person on whom a safety and health obligation is imposed may be subject to more than 1 safety and health obligation.
Example— A person may be a coal mine operator, contractor and supplier of plant at the same time for a single coal mine and be subject to obligations in each of the capacities. 36 Person not relieved of obligations To remove doubt, it is declared that nothing in this Act that imposes a safety and health obligation on a person relieves another person of the person’s safety and health obligations under this Act.

sections.heading: How obligation can be discharged if regulation or
sections.text:
recognised standard made
(1) If a regulation prescribes a way of achieving an acceptable level of risk, a person may discharge the person’s safety and health obligation in relation to the risk only by following the prescribed way.
(2) If a regulation prohibits exposure to a risk, a person may discharge the person’s safety and health obligation in relation to the risk only by ensuring the prohibition is not contravened.
(3) Subject to subsections (1) and (2), if a recognised standard states a way or ways of achieving an acceptable level of risk, a person discharges the person’s safety and health obligation in relation to the risk only by—
(a) adopting and following a stated way; or
(b) adopting and following another way that achieves a level of risk that is equal to or better than the acceptable level.

sections.heading: How obligations can be discharged if no regulation or
sections.text:
recognised standard made
(1) This section applies if there is no regulation or recognised standard prescribing or stating a way to discharge the person’s safety and health obligation in relation to a risk.
(2) The person may choose an appropriate way to discharge the person’s safety and health obligation in relation to the risk.
(3) However, the person discharges the person’s safety and health obligation in relation to the risk only if the person takes reasonable precautions, and exercises proper diligence, to ensure the obligation is discharged. health obligations of persons

sections.heading: Obligations of persons generally
Additional obligations
Obligations of holders
sections.text:
(1) This section applies if the holder for a coal mine proposes to appoint under section 53 another person as coal mine operator for the mine.
(2) The holder must—
(a) inform the proposed coal mine operator, by notice, of all relevant information available to the holder that may help the proposed coal mine operator—
(i) ensure the site senior executive for the coal mine develops and implements a safety and health management system for the mine; and
(ii) prepare and implement principal hazard management plans for the mine; and
(b) include in the contract appointing the coal mine operator an obligation on the operator—
(i) to establish a safety and health management system for the mine; and
(ii) other than for exploration activities under an exploration permit or mineral development licence—to be a party to a mines rescue agreement.

crumbs.division: Division 3 Obligations of holders, coal mine

sections.heading: Obligations of coal mine operators

crumbs.division: Division 3 Obligations of holders, coal mine

sections.heading: Obligations of site senior executive for coal mine

crumbs.division: Division 3 Obligations of holders, coal mine

sections.heading: Obligations of contractors

crumbs.division: Division 3 Obligations of holders, coal mine

sections.heading: Obligations of designers, manufacturers, importers and
sections.text:
suppliers of plant etc. for use at coal mines
(1) A designer or importer of plant for use at a coal mine has an obligation to ensure the plant is designed so that, when used properly, the risk to persons from the use of the plant is at an acceptable level.
(2) A manufacturer or importer of plant for use at a coal mine has an obligation to ensure the plant is constructed so that, when used properly, the risk to persons from the use of the plant is at an acceptable level.
(3) A designer, manufacturer or importer of plant for use at a coal mine has an obligation to ensure the plant undergoes appropriate levels of testing and examination to ensure compliance with the obligation imposed by subsection (1) or
(2).
(4) Also, a designer, manufacturer, importer or supplier of plant for use at a coal mine has the following obligations—
(a) to take all reasonable steps to ensure appropriate information about the safe use of the plant is available, including information about the maintenance necessary for the safe use of the plant;
(b) if the designer, manufacturer, importer or supplier becomes aware of a hazard or defect associated with the plant that may create an unacceptable level of risk to users of the plant, to inform the chief inspector of—
(i) the nature of the hazard or defect and its significance; and
(ii) any modifications or controls of which the designer, manufacturer, importer or supplier is aware that have been developed to eliminate or correct the hazard or defect or manage the risk; and
(iii) the name of each coal mine operator or contractor to whom the designer, manufacturer, importer or supplier has supplied the plant; and
(iv) the steps taken to notify the coal mine operators and contractors about the matters mentioned in subparagraphs (i) and (ii);
(c) to take the action the chief inspector reasonably requires to prevent the use of unsafe plant anywhere.
Example of subsection (4)(c)— The chief inspector may require a designer, manufacturer, importer or supplier of plant to recall the plant to prevent its use.
(5) For subsection (4)(a), information is appropriate if the information states—
(a) the use for which the plant has been designed and tested; and
(b) any conditions that must be followed if the plant is to be used safely so that risk to persons is at an acceptable level.
(6) If a supplier of plant becomes aware of a hazard or defect associated with the plant the supplier has supplied to a coal mine operator for a coal mine or to a contractor for use at a coal mine, that may create an unacceptable level of risk to users of the plant, the supplier has an obligation to take all reasonable steps to inform the coal mine operator or contractor—
(a) of the nature of the hazard or defect and its significance; and
(b) any modifications or controls the supplier is aware of that have been developed to eliminate or correct the hazard or defect or manage the risk.

crumbs.division: Division 3 Obligations of holders, coal mine

sections.heading: Obligations of erectors and installers of plant
sections.text:
An erector or installer of plant at a coal mine has an obligation—
(a) to erect or install the plant in a way that is safe and does not expose persons at the mine to an unacceptable level of risk; and
(b) to ensure nothing about the way the plant was erected or installed makes it unsafe or likely to expose persons at the mine to an unacceptable level of risk when used properly.

crumbs.division: Division 3 Obligations of holders, coal mine

sections.heading: Obligations of designers, constructors and erectors of
sections.text:
earthworks
(1) A designer of earthworks at a coal mine has an obligation to ensure the earthworks are designed so that, when used properly, the risk to persons from the use of the earthworks is at an acceptable level.
Examples of earthworks— tailings dam, berm
(2) A constructor or erector of earthworks at a coal mine has an obligation—
(a) to construct or erect the earthworks in a way that is safe and does not expose persons to an unacceptable level of risk; and
(b) to ensure nothing about the way the earthworks are constructed or erected makes the earthworks unsafe or likely to expose persons to an unacceptable level of risk when used properly.

crumbs.division: Division 3 Obligations of holders, coal mine

sections.heading: Obligations of manufacturers, importers and suppliers of
sections.text:
substances for use at coal mines
(1) A manufacturer or importer of a substance for use at a coal mine has the following obligations—
(a) to ensure the substance is safe so that, when used properly, the risk to persons from the use of the substance is at an acceptable level;
(b) to ensure the substance undergoes appropriate levels of testing and examination to ensure compliance with the obligation imposed by paragraph (a).
(2) Also, a manufacturer, importer or supplier of a substance for use at a coal mine has the following obligations—
(a) to ensure appropriate information about the safe use, storage and disposal of the substance is provided with the substance;
(b) if the manufacturer, importer or supplier becomes aware of a hazard or defect associated with the substance that may create an unacceptable level of risk to users of the substance, to inform the chief inspector of—
(i) the nature of the hazard or defect and its significance; and
(ii) any modifications or controls of which the manufacturer, importer or supplier is aware that have been developed to eliminate or correct the hazard or defect or manage the risk; and
(iii) the name of each coal mine operator or contractor to whom the manufacturer, importer or supplier has supplied the substance; and
(iv) the steps taken to notify the coal mine operators and contractors about the matters mentioned in subparagraphs (i) and (ii);
(c) to take the action the chief inspector reasonably requires to prevent the use of an unsafe substance at a coal mine.
Example of subsection (2)(c)— The chief inspector may require a manufacturer, importer or supplier of a substance to recall the substance to prevent its use.
(3) For subsection (2)(a), information is appropriate if the information clearly identifies the substance and states—
(a) the precautions, if any, to be taken for the safe use, storage or disposal of the substance; and
(b) the risks, if any, associated with the use, storage or disposal of the substance.
(4) If a supplier of a substance for use at a coal mine becomes aware of a hazard or defect associated with the substance that may create an unacceptable level of risk to users of the substance, the supplier has an obligation to take all reasonable steps to inform each coal mine operator or contractor to whom the supplier has supplied the substance of—
(a) the nature of the hazard or defect and its significance; and
(b) any modifications or controls the supplier is aware of that have been developed to eliminate or correct the hazard or defect or manage the risk. corporations

crumbs.division: Division 3 Obligations of holders, coal mine

sections.heading: Obligation of officers of corporations
sections.text:
(1) If a corporation has an obligation under this Act, an officer of the corporation must exercise due diligence to ensure the corporation complies with the obligation.
(2) An officer of a corporation may be convicted or found guilty of an offence under this Act relating to an obligation of the officer whether or not the corporation has been convicted or found guilty of an offence under this Act relating to an obligation of the corporation.
(3) In this section, due diligence includes taking reasonable steps—
(a) to acquire and keep up-to-date knowledge of mine safety and health matters; and
(b) to gain an understanding of the nature of coal mining operations at a coal mine and generally of the hazards, risks and critical controls associated with those operations; and
(c) to ensure the corporation has available for use, and uses, appropriate resources and processes to eliminate or minimise risks to safety and health from work carried out as part of coal mining operations; and
(d) to ensure the corporation has appropriate processes for receiving and considering information regarding incidents, hazards, risks and critical controls and responding in a timely way to that information; and
(e) to ensure the corporation has, and implements, processes for complying with any obligation of the corporation under this Act; and
(f) to verify the provision and use of the resources and processes mentioned in paragraphs (c) to (e).
Example for paragraph (f)— If the corporation is a coal mine operator, verifying the provision and use of the resources and processes to ensure the operator complies with the requirement under section 41(1)(g) (including, for example, having regard to each report given by the operator in relation to an audit of the effectiveness and implementation of the mine’s safety and health management system).
(4) In this section— officer, of a corporation, does not include a person appointed as, or whose position reports directly or indirectly to, the site senior executive for a coal mine.

sections.heading: Defences for div 2, 3 or 3A
sections.text:
(1) It is a defence in a proceeding against a person for a contravention of an obligation imposed on the person under division 2, 3 or 3A in relation to a risk for the person to prove—
(a) if a regulation has been made about the way to achieve an acceptable level of risk—the person followed the way prescribed in the regulation to prevent the contravention; or
(b) subject to paragraph (a), if a recognised standard has been made stating a way or ways to achieve an acceptable level of a risk—
(i) that the person adopted and followed a stated way to prevent the contravention; or
(ii) that the person adopted and followed another way that achieved a level of risk that is equal to or better than the acceptable level to prevent the contravention; or
(c) if no regulation or recognised standard prescribes or states a way to discharge the person’s safety and health obligation in relation to the risk—that the person took reasonable precautions and exercised proper diligence to prevent the contravention.
(2) Also, it is a defence in a proceeding against a person for an offence against section 34 for the person to prove that the commission of the offence was due to causes over which the person had no control.
(3) The Criminal Code, sections 23 and 24, do not apply in relation to a contravention of section 34.
(4) In this section, a reference to a recognised standard is a reference to the recognised standard in force at the time of the contravention.

sections.heading: Definitions for part
sections.text:
(1) In this part— conduct means an act or omission to perform an act. employer, for a coal mine, means—
(a) a person who employs or otherwise engages a coal mine worker for the coal mine; or
(b) a person who arranges for a coal mine worker to work for the coal mine, including for example, a labour hire agency; or
(c) the coal mine operator for the coal mine; or
(d) the holder for the coal mine. executive officer, of a corporation, means a person who is concerned with, or takes part in, the corporation’s management, whether or not the person is a director or the person’s position is given the name of executive officer. senior officer, of an employer for a coal mine, means—
(a) if the employer is a corporation—an executive officer of the corporation; or
(b) otherwise—the holder of an executive position (however described) in relation to the employer who makes, or takes part in making, decisions affecting all, or a substantial part, of the employer’s functions.
(2) For this part, a person’s conduct causes death if it substantially contributes to the death.

sections.heading: Exception for the Criminal Code, s 23
sections.text: The Criminal Code, section 23 does not apply in relation to an offence against this part.

sections.heading: Industrial manslaughter—employer
sections.text:
(1) An employer for a coal mine commits an offence if—
(a) a coal mine worker—
(i) dies in the course of carrying out work at the coal mine; or
(ii) is injured in the course of carrying out work at the coal mine and later dies; and
(b) the employer’s conduct causes the death of the coal mine worker; and
(c) the employer is negligent about causing the death of the coal mine worker by the conduct.
Maximum penalty—
(a) for an individual—20 years imprisonment; or
(b) for a body corporate—100,000 penalty units.
Note— See section 261 in relation to imputing to a body corporate particular conduct of officers, employees or agents of the body corporate.
(2) An offence against subsection (1) is a crime.

sections.heading: Industrial manslaughter—senior officer
sections.text:
(1) A senior officer of an employer for a coal mine commits an offence if—
(a) a coal mine worker—
(i) dies in the course of carrying out work at the coal mine; or
(ii) is injured in the course of carrying out work at the coal mine and later dies; and
(b) the senior officer’s conduct causes the death of the coal mine worker; and
(c) the senior officer is negligent about causing the death of the coal mine worker by the conduct.
Maximum penalty—20 years imprisonment.
(2) An offence against subsection (1) is a crime. of coal mines

crumbs.part: Part 4 Provisions about the operation of coal mines

sections.heading: Notices by holder
sections.text:
(1) Before coal mining operations start at a coal mine or a separate part of a surface mine, the holder for the mine must give the inspector for the region in which the mine is situated notice of—
(a) the name and address of the coal mine operator for the mine or part; and
(b) the name of, and a description of the land (including its boundary) comprising, the mine or part; and
(c) the date on which operations are to start at the mine or part.
Maximum penalty—40 penalty units.
(2) Subsection (1)(b) and (c) do not apply to exploration activities under an exploration permit or mineral development licence.
(3) The holder must not change the following for a coal mine without first giving the inspector for the region in which the mine is situated notice—
(a) the coal mine operator;
(b) the name of the mine.
Maximum penalty for subsection (3)—40 penalty units.

sections.heading: Notices by coal mine operator
sections.text:
(1) Before coal mining operations start at a coal mine, the coal mine operator must give the inspector for the region in which the coal mine is situated notice of the name and address of the site senior executive for the mine.
Maximum penalty—40 penalty units.
(2) Also, the coal mine operator must, within 7 days after the appointment, give the inspector for the region notice of the following appointments including the name and address of the person appointed—
(a) the appointment of a new site senior executive;
(b) an appointment under section 57.
Maximum penalty—40 penalty units.
(3) When land is added to or omitted from a coal mine, the coal mine operator must, within 1 month after the addition or omission, give to the inspector for the region in which the mine is situated written particulars of the land (including its boundary) added or omitted.
Maximum penalty—40 penalty units.
(4) If coal mining operations permanently stop at the coal mine, the coal mine operator must, within 28 days after the operations permanently stop, give the inspector for the region in which the coal mine is situated notice of the date on which the operations permanently stopped.
Maximum penalty—100 penalty units.

crumbs.part: Part 4 Provisions about the operation of coal mines

sections.heading: Notice of management structure
sections.text:
Before coal mining operations start at a coal mine, the site senior executive must give a copy of the management structure the site senior executive must document under section 55 to the inspector for the region in which the mine is situated.
Maximum penalty—40 penalty units.

crumbs.part: Part 4 Provisions about the operation of coal mines

sections.heading: Notice about exploration activities
sections.text:
If exploration activities are to be carried out on land under an exploration permit or mineral development licence, the coal mine operator must give the inspector for the region in which the land subject to the exploration permit or mineral development licence is situated notice of the nature of the intended activity and the planned start date and duration of the activity.
Maximum penalty—40 penalty units.

crumbs.part: Part 4 Provisions about the operation of coal mines

sections.heading: Notice about underground gasification activities
sections.text:
(1) This section applies if the site senior executive for a coal mine gives the chief inspector notice that particular exploration activities at the coal mine under an exploration permit are underground gasification activities.
(2) The chief inspector may by notice declare the activities to be underground gasification activities, with the agreement of the chief inspector, petroleum and gas.
(3) The chief inspector must give the site senior executive a copy of the notice.
(4) In this section— chief inspector, petroleum and gas means the chief inspector under the Petroleum and Gas (Production and Safety) Act 2004.

crumbs.part: Part 4 Provisions about the operation of coal mines

sections.heading: Appointment of coal mine operator
sections.text:
(1) The holder for a coal mine may, by written contract, appoint a person as the coal mine operator for the mine or, if the mine is or includes a separate part of a surface mine, the separate part.
(2) An appointment of a person as coal mine operator for a part of a coal mine that is not a separate part of a surface mine is ineffective.

crumbs.part: Part 4 Provisions about the operation of coal mines

sections.heading: Limitations on appointment of site senior executive
sections.text:
(1) A coal mine operator for a coal mine or for a separate part of a surface mine must not appoint more than 1 site senior executive for the mine or for the part for which the person is coal mine operator.
Maximum penalty—500 penalty units.
(2) A coal mine operator must not appoint a person to be site senior executive for more than 1 coal mine.
Maximum penalty—500 penalty units.
(3) However, a person may be appointed to be site senior executive for more than 1 coal mine if—
(a) the mines are part of a mining project; or
(b) the mines consist only of exploration activities under an exploration permit, mineral development licence or mining lease; or
(c) the mines are adjacent and on-site activities for winning coal are carried on at only 1 of the mines; or
(d) the mines comprise mines forming part of a mining project and adjacent mines, and the adjacent mines consist only of exploration activities under an exploration permit, mineral development licence or mining lease.
(4) A coal mine operator must not appoint a person to be site senior executive for a coal mine unless the person holds—
